citations.cited_for: An LLC takes the citizenship of each of its members for diversity jurisdiction, not its state of formation or principal place of business

first_check.explanation: Carden v. Arkoma Associates, 494 U.S. 185 (1990), is correctly cited. It holds that for diversity purposes the citizenship of an artificial entity other than a corporation depends on the citizenship of all its members, and it rejects looking only to some members or treating the entity as a citizen of its state of organization. The case itself involved a limited partnership, not an LLC. Courts of appeals apply Carden's general rule for artificial entities to LLCs, so citing it as the source of the LLC member-citizenship rule is standard practice. A 'see' signal or an explanatory parenthetical would make that clearer.

citations.authority: Texas law on exemplary damages (no statutory cap for these tort claims)
citations.cited_for: Punitive damages may be available under Texas law for fraud and breach of fiduciary duty; Texas imposes no statutory cap on exemplary damages for non-economic tort claims of this nature
citations.context: Punitive damages may also be available under Texas law for claims sounding in fraud and breach of fiduciary duty. Texas does not impose a statutory cap on exemplary damages for non-economic tort claims of this nature.

first_check.explanation: Texas allows exemplary damages for fraud, so that part of the memo is correct. But the memo is wrong to say Texas has no statutory cap for fraud or breach of fiduciary duty claims. Section 41.008(b) caps exemplary damages at the greater of $200,000 or two times economic damages plus noneconomic damages up to $750,000. The cap is lifted only under § 41.008(c), which requires conduct that would be one of the listed felonies, committed knowingly or intentionally. The list includes misapplication of fiduciary property (Penal Code § 32.45), commercial bribery (§ 32.43), and felony theft. Fraud and breach of fiduciary duty claims as such are therefore capped unless the plaintiff proves an enumerated felony.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: § 41.008(b): "Exemplary damages awarded against a defendant may not exceed an amount equal to the greater of: (1)(A) two times the amount of economic damages; plus (B) an amount equal to any noneconomic damages found by the jury, not to exceed $750,000; or (2) $200,000." § 41.008(c) exempts listed felony conduct committed knowingly or intentionally (e.g., § 32.45 misapplication of fiduciary property).

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. The intake memo says Texas imposes 'no statutory cap on exemplary damages for non-economic tort claims of this nature' (fraud and breach of fiduciary duty). Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 41.008(b) caps exemplary damages at the greater of '(A) two times the amount of economic damages; plus (B) an amount equal to any noneconomic damages found by the jury, not to exceed $750,000' or '$200,000.' Under § 41.008(c), the cap is lifted only where the conduct would be one of the listed felonies, committed knowingly or intentionally. The list includes 'Section 32.43 (Commercial Bribery),' 'Section 32.45 (Misapplication of Fiduciary Property...),' 'Section 32.46 (Fraudulent Securing of Document Execution),' forgery, and felony theft. Fraud and fiduciary-duty tort claims as such are therefore capped unless the plaintiff proves an enumerated felony. The memo's categorical no-cap statement misstates the statute. The statement appears to be an error deliberately planted in the task's source documents, but as a statement of law it is mischaracterized.
